subject: physics
question: Explain river and boat problems for JEE using this example: a river 100 m wide flows east at 3 m/s, and a boat heads due north at 4 m/s relative to the water. How do the crossing time, the drift and the heading to go straight across work?

givens.sourceText: boat heads due north at 4 m/s relative to the water

qualitativeClaims.claim: Crossing time depends only on the river width and the boat's velocity component perpendicular to the banks; the current does not affect it.
Drift is the downstream displacement caused by the current during the crossing; the boat lands 75 m east of the point directly opposite.
To go straight across, the boat must head upstream (west of north) at angle theta so its upstream component cancels the current.
qualitativeClaims.expected: theta = arcsin(v_r/v_b) = 48.59 deg west of north

qualitativeClaims.claim: When heading straight across, the resultant speed across the river is reduced to sqrt(v_b^2 - v_r^2), so the crossing takes longer (37.8 s vs 25 s).
Heading due north gives the minimum crossing time; heading upstream to cancel drift gives the shortest path but a longer time.
qualitativeClaims.expected: t_min = 25 s (due north); straight-across path takes 37.8 s

qualitativeClaims.claim: Straight-across heading is possible only if v_b > v_r; here 4 > 3 so it is achievable.

assumptions: River current is uniform and steady at 3 m/s east everywhere
Boat speed relative to water is constant at 4 m/s
River banks are parallel and straight, 100 m apart
East is +x, north is +y; boat starts at the south bank
No wind, waves, or acceleration; boat instantly reaches heading

subject: physics
question: Explain river and boat problems for JEE using this example: a river 100 m wide flows east at 3 m/s, and a boat heads due north at 4 m/s relative to the water. How do the crossing time, the drift and the heading to go straight across work?

givens.sourceText: boat heads due north at 4 m/s relative to the water

qualitativeClaims.claim: Crossing time depends only on the river width and the boat's velocity component perpendicular to the banks (here the full 4 m/s northward), not on the current.
While crossing, the current carries the boat downstream (east); drift equals current speed times crossing time.
qualitativeClaims.expected: d = v_r * t = 75 m east of the point directly opposite the start

qualitativeClaims.claim: The boat's resultant velocity relative to ground is the vector sum of 4 m/s north and 3 m/s east, magnitude 5 m/s, directed about 36.87° east of north.
qualitativeClaims.expected: v_ground = sqrt(v_b^2 + v_r^2) = 5 m/s at arctan(3/4) ≈ 36.87° east of north

qualitativeClaims.claim: To go straight across (zero drift), the boat must head upstream (west of north) so its eastward component cancels the current: v_b sinθ = v_r.
qualitativeClaims.expected: θ = arcsin(v_r / v_b) = arcsin(3/4) ≈ 48.59° west of north

qualitativeClaims.claim: When heading upstream to cancel drift, the effective crossing speed drops to v_b cosθ, so the crossing takes longer than 25 s.
qualitativeClaims.expected: t_straight = w / (v_b cosθ) = 100 / sqrt(4^2 - 3^2) = 100 / sqrt(7) ≈ 37.8 s

qualitativeClaims.claim: JEE key idea: minimum time crossing means heading straight across (perpendicular to banks) and accepting drift; minimum drift (zero) means aiming upstream, costing more time.
qualitativeClaims.expected: Fastest crossing: head due north, t = 25 s, drift 75 m. Straight-across path: head 48.59° upstream, t ≈ 37.8 s, drift 0.

lawIds: kinematics with constant velocity (x = v t)
condition for zero resultant downstream component
assumptions: Current speed is uniform across the river's width
Boat's speed relative to water is constant at 4 m/s
East is +x, north is +y; banks are straight and parallel
No wind, acceleration, or other forces affect the boat
